content: Abacavir is associated with a risk of a severe, potentially fatal allergic reaction. Before starting or restarting this medication, your doctor should perform a blood test to assess your risk. If the test indicates a high risk, you must not take abacavir, and your doctor will discuss alternative treatments with you. Symptoms of an allergic reaction may include rash, itching or swelling (especially of the face, tongue, or throat), severe dizziness, difficulty breathing, fever, extreme fatigue, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, muscle aches, sore throat, or cough. If you experience any of these symptoms, seek medical attention immediately. If you have discontinued abacavir due to an allergic reaction, you must never take it again, as this could result in death. Inform all your healthcare providers if you have stopped taking abacavir due to an allergic reaction, and properly dispose of any unused medication. This medication is used in combination with other HIV medications to control HIV infection. It works by reducing the amount of HIV in your body, allowing your immune system to function more effectively. This decreases the risk of HIV-related complications, such as new infections or cancer, and improves your quality of life. However, abacavir is not a cure for HIV. To reduce the risk of transmitting HIV to others, continue taking all HIV medications exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Use effective barrier methods, such as latex or polyurethane condoms or dental dams, during sexual activity as directed by your doctor. Do not share personal items like needles, syringes, toothbrushes, or razors that may have come into contact with blood or other body fluids. Read the Medication Guide and Warning Card provided by your pharmacist before starting abacavir and each time you get a refill. Carry the Warning Card with you at all times. Take this medication by mouth, with or without food, as directed by your doctor, usually once or twice daily. If you are using the liquid form, measure the dose carefully with a special measuring device or spoon. The dosage is based on your medical condition and response to treatment. If you stop taking abacavir, even for a short time, and then restart it, you have an increased risk of developing a severe, potentially fatal allergic reaction. Refill your medication before you run out, and do not stop treatment unless directed by your doctor. It is crucial to take this medication (and other HIV medications) exactly as prescribed. Do not skip doses, increase your dose, take it more frequently than prescribed, or stop taking it without your doctor’s guidance. For optimal effectiveness, take this medication at evenly spaced intervals. Common side effects may include trouble sleeping or loss of appetite. Remember that this medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. As your immune system strengthens, it may begin to fight off infections you already had, potentially causing disease symptoms to reappear. You may also experience symptoms if your immune system becomes overactive. These reactions can occur at any time, either shortly after starting HIV treatment or months later. Rarely, abacavir has caused severe, sometimes fatal liver problems and a buildup of lactic acid in the blood (lactic acidosis). These serious side effects are more common in women and obese patients. This is not a complete list of possible side effects. In the U.S., contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. In Canada, consult your doctor for medical advice about side effects. Before taking abacavir, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it or if you have any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that can cause allergic reactions or other problems. Abacavir may increase your risk of a heart attack. Discuss the risks and benefits of treatment with your doctor, as well as ways to lower your risk of heart disease. Inform your doctor if you are pregnant before using this medication. Treatment can reduce the risk of transmitting HIV to your baby. This medication passes into breast milk. Drug interactions may alter how your medications work or increase your risk of serious side effects. This document does not include all possible drug interactions. Keep a list of all the products you use (including prescription and nonprescription drugs and herbal products) and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Do not take this medication with other medications that contain abacavir. Check the labels on all your prescription medications to ensure they do not contain abacavir. In case of overdose, if someone has serious symptoms such as passing out or trouble breathing, call 911. Otherwise, contact a poison control center immediately. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222. While taking this medication, lab and/or medical tests (such as liver function, viral load, T-cell counts) should be performed regularly. Keep all medical and lab appointments. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is near the time of the next dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Do not double the dose to catch up. Store abacavir solution or tablets at room temperature, away from light and moisture. The solution may also be stored in the refrigerator but should not be frozen. Over time, the solution may change from clear or yellow to brown. Do not store this medication in the bathroom. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. This information is a summary and does not contain all possible details about this product. It does not guarantee that this product is safe, effective, or appropriate for you. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this product and your specific health needs.
